game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Description[/h1]

Orwell is a visual novel that puts you in the shoes of a Big Brother employee: you are tasked with spying on people and uploading to the system anything suspicious. Unlike most visual novels, you are not presented here with walls of text followed by lists of choices. Rather, your interaction with the game and its unfolding story goes solely through the gimmick of uploading the data chunks you find (or not). By picking among conflicting data chunks or by choosing not to upload some sensitive information, you impact the story in small and big ways.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
[*] Fresh interaction gimmick that goes very well with the theme
[*] Credible writing with many characters each having their own style of speech
[*] Interesting choices going WAY beyond the good/bad dichotomy
[*] Decent art style
[*] Fair amount of consequences to choices made, though the game remains linear
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
[*] Notification system takes some getting used to ([spoiler]the system will sometimes find old information suddenly relevant, requiring you to regularly browse through the lists of documents to make sure no red star has popped[/spoiler])
[*] Because all chats and phone calls are delivered sloooooowly (and I found no way to speed them up), replaying the game to get the achievements or test other choices is a bit of a chore
[*] Political messages are (very) thinly veiled and might annoy (or even anger?) some players
[/list]

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

Do you hate it when someone tries to convey a political message artistically and ends up as subtle as a bull in a china shop? If so, stay away from this game. You're going to hate it.

Still here? OK, here's an idea: put yourself in the shoes of an orwellian enforcer and imagine the consequences of government trampling all over freedom, privacy and presumption of innocence.

Interested? Then try Orwell. Go in expecting a fresh visual novel and a politically charged (to the point of being heavy-handed at times) thought experiment. There is much to like.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Game Summary: [/h1] 
This game doesn't fit into most normal game conventions and acts more like a cautionary tale.  By allowing the gamer to take the seat of a possible government agent in a program giving you so much power and access over people's lives, it lets you determine what you take away from it.  Is it a necessary evil for the government to have this much depth and access to what people are posting online, downloaded on their various devices, and talking about in their phone calls?  Or is that question alone already pushing too far, as people have an inherent right to privacy?  Wisely the game developer merely posits this to its audience, instead of preaching what is or isn't appropriate behavior in the 21st Century and beyond.  


[h1] Pros: [/h1] 
•	The first playthrough where I was intruding so far into people's lives made me feel uncomfortable.  Not scared or tense, just somewhat uncomfortable.  I think it's because invading people's privacy to this extent, knowing how easily the same thing could happen to you, is rather unsettling.  Medical records and mental health histories, various profiles and online communities you participate in (theoretically behind an alias), personal conversations and chats, all available for someone to read through.  For someone to comb through for any signs of instability, derangement, or evidence that this person isn't a law-abiding citizen, but a dirty crook.  This is dangerously close to criminalizing people for wrong-think.  
•	This game shines in its story and writing, because the characters feel real.  Their various profiles and conversations, how they become both paranoid and angry, but still only guessing at how bad things already are regarding the government's intrusion into their lives.  It gives the game a greater sense of reality and immersion, which is key.  They may not be rocket scientists, but they do take steps to avoid being screwed over, though if you're being a good big brother, it's already too late for them.  
•	I love that what I choose to upload can have a pretty big impact on how what the characters are saying and doing is interpreted.  It can either be seen as the acts of an innocent person, or the pattern of someone who's a low-down crook.  It raises the question of how any of us would look from the outside to someone who'd see all of our online activity.
•	The music acts as ambient background.  It's very low-key, and could theoretically be the sort of soft tune a government office would play to keep employees from getting too antsy.  This is for the most part, but when the climax of each day/act builds, then it picks up and gets you on edge.


[h1] Cons: [/h1] 
• 	Though it would take more time in both development and gameplay, it'd be nice if there were more people for you to look into who turned out to be red herrings.  It's not necessarily enjoyable being led astray, but it'd help sharpen the point of the game.  If you were being paranoid and looking at people through the lens of criminalizing everyone, you'd waste time and resources chasing false leads.  If you put on kids gloves and rationalized every viable threat as a misunderstanding, you'd let dangerous people slip on through.  What people say and mean aren't always the same, and one person's harmless rant is another's death threat.  
•	*Semi-Spoiler* I think one downside of the story is that all the key players are not inherently innocent.  They all have something significant to cover up, a reasonable way of implicating them for a crime and leading to their detention.  If they were merely guilty by association, and small phrases and statements were being pulled together to paint them as guilty, I think that would have had a stronger impact.  Otherwise, with how it is here, locking everybody up is justified.  You aren't throwing someone in jail who's wholly innocent.
•	Ironically, with how the last day plays out, you get so much material to look at, but are strictly limited on how much you can upload.  I get the idea of building tension this way, but I think it goes against what the game was going for.  The dilemma of the game wasn't in having to make a decision with so little information, but at digging for far too much, and falsely implicating innocent people on what you could piece together.  
•	Where the game suffers is through further playthroughs, as you see what happens if you try things a bit differently.  Since you're familiar with the characters, storyline, and reading their messages, it'd be nice if those could be sped up, instead of having to wait.  The chats are fairly crisp-paced considering they're supposed to be happening real-time, but it bogs down when you've seen it before.
•	Early in the game, video footage was used, and I thought that was going to come up again later.  I was quite disappointed that it only had a place in the game once, and I do feel misled that everything you analyze in the game is just text, whether a call, chat, or profile.
•	It'd be nice if some of the items which are definitively pointless and not useful anymore would be cleared away.  For instance, all the random news clips and headlines, since most of them had no pertinence to the exploration for more information.  
•	Sometimes I had a really hard time dragging points of interest into profiles or disabling them.  The controls were a bit floaty and annoying to work with.


[h1] Conclusion: [/h1] 
Whether we like it or not, whatever we post online is going to exist indefinitely.  Since so much information is out there, it does raise the issue of who would be keeping track of these matters, who might be lurking without our knowledge to try and keep tabs over us.  Whether it's the government or not, people can do some pretty sketchy things with computers, and this knowledge and power is a great temptation, tool, and force.  This game acts as a simulation for what can be done with that kind of power.  A bumbling buffoon who doesn't take it seriously, could allow guilty parties to slip out of facing justice.  An overly authoritarian and distrustful person could throw people behind bars for any minor infraction.  True, laws may have been broken, but should we throw away privacy and autonomy to catch such small fries?  We'd be foolish to hand over such power carelessly, as it could be so easily abused, but total restriction could also prevent heinous monsters from being caught and prosecuted.  These are hefty matters worthy of being discussed in the public sphere, and this game highlights both sides of that discussion.  If you're looking for a game in a conventional sense, you'd be disappointed, but if you're open to an experience with an important message at its core, Orwell has a lot to offer.  

Be careful if you write a reply or comment on this review.  You don't know who could be reading it.  It's alright if you don't necessarily agree with everything the government does, but don't be overly critical and certainly don't call for a revolution or anything CRAZY like that.  We'd HATE for there to be a group trying to overthrow the government, right?  Oh crap, I hear them at my door.  They're on to me!  Fight while you still can, don't be compliant, resist, fight on, fi-!  *Device has been disconnected*

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h3][i]“War is peace. Freedom is slavery. Ignorance is strength.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]


Even if you haven't read anything by George Orwell, you've probably heard about 1984. The dystopia the author foresaw has undoubtedly materialized in the modern world, as most readers of the book like to point out. This assertion is without doubt true; even if you only use the internet for personal purposes, there are still a lot of data crumbs left behind. You can never be certain if someone is keeping an eye on your every online move, whether it be a post about a recent vacation, a comment made on a forum, or the address you use to sign emails. 
This is precisely what Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You promises: it is a game about a reality that nobody wants to face but that hangs in the air.

[h3][i]“The consequences of every act are included in the act itself.”[/i] - George Orwell[/h3]

The game takes place in the capital of a fictional country called The Nation, where on April 12th, 2017, a terrorist attack occurs: a bomb detonates in the famous Freedom Plaza, destroying a statue and killing several people. At the same time, the police receive a note containing the first three stanzas of a German folk song called The Thoughts are Free.

In 2012, The Party, a paternalistic government that leads The Nation, passed the Safety Bill, which gave the government complete freedom over citizens' personal data and the ability to spy on them using a surveillance system called Orwell. This is where your involvement with The Nation begins.
You are the first person who has been selected to be an investigator - a citizen outside of The Nation, who will use Orwell to uncover as much data about a person as possible. You are being accompanied by an Advisor, who will connect you to the authorities. 

The plot is essentially a classic detective whodunit story told in five chapters; throughout the game, multiple suspects will emerge, and your job will be to determine each person's involvement and, in the end, find the perpetrator(s) - or is it?
The aforementioned data (which the game refers to as datachucks) gathering is the game's main essence and gameplay mechanic - you have access to a wide range of websites, phones, e-mail addresses, and even computers, where you must find information related to your lead. This isn't a difficult task because the game highlights them in blue or yellow; the latter indicates a data collision, and you must determine which is the correct data.

A few things should be kept in mind with this mechanic: first, it is completely irreversible - once you upload something in the system, there is no way to change it, and the story will proceed accordingly; second, you do not need to upload every possible datachunk - at first, the game forces you to do this, but later you must be careful what you upload; and third, the game is actually a choose-your-own-adventure with a detective façade - given that there are multiple endings, your choices will have a heavy impact on the story.

Orwell's strength is the moral uncertainty it contains. Players will have to weigh the pros and cons of sharing new information with the people they're investigating versus keeping it to themselves as they gather additional evidence. Because of this, players will feel more invested in the game and more emotionally connected to their choices.

[h3][i]“But if thought corrupts language, language can also corrupt thought.” [/i]- George Orwell[/h3]

One of the game's greatest strengths is its immersive and atmospheric presentation. The dark and minimalist art style, combined with a haunting original soundtrack, sets the perfect tone for an oppressive world governed by The Party. The user interface is sleek and intuitive, allowing easy navigation of the vast amount of information at your disposal. Towards the end of the game, the interface will get much more crowded; however, the game displays a red icon next to a document where new data chunks can be found. Furthermore, the game's soundtrack perfectly complements the dystopian atmosphere, with haunting melodies and industrial beats that immerse players in the world of surveillance and control. 

Orwell does, however, have a few minor flaws. As the investigation progresses through a series of data-mining tasks, the gameplay can feel slow at times. Some players, particularly those who prefer more action-oriented experiences, may find these moments tedious. Furthermore, while the game encourages players to take different paths, the overall impact of your choices on the narrative can feel somewhat limited, leaving some room for a more dynamic and personalized experience unexplored.
The length of the game is another aspect of the experience that could be improved. The story is interesting and the decisions are weighty, yet the game is over in a matter of hours and it left me craving for more. The game's depth of topic and potential for replay may have benefited from more content or branching routes.



[h3][i]“Freedom is the freedom to say that two plus two make four. If that is granted, all else follows.”[/i]
 - George Orwell[/h3]

Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You is a fascinating and unsettling adventure that delves into the moral issues raised by omniscient monitoring and the misuse of authority. A standout in the narrative-driven genre, thanks to its engaging tale, accessible gameplay, and morally weighty choices. Even though it's not particularly long and has a few weaker points, it's a must-play if you enjoy engaging stories set in dystopian futures.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You (in short, Orwell) is a five-part episodic narrative-driven mystery video game by Osmotic Studios set in a dystopian world in which the player assumes the role of a governmental operative who monitors surveillance sources to discovery national security threats. The game is named after the famed anti-totalitarian writer George Orwell and is inspired by themes established by his magnum opus novel, 1984.

The story in Orwell takes place in a country named The Nation which is governed by a contemporary authoritarian government known as The Party. Due to a series of events in the past, The Party passed the Safety Bill which expanded the government's capability to spy on its citizens in the name of national security. To accomplish this, the Ministry of Security, at the helm of Secretary of Security Catherine Delacroix, built a secret surveillance system codenamed Orwell. After a successful application and being selected from a pool of candidates, the player takes the role of an outsourced Orwell investigator who lives outside The Nation and is tasked, with the help of an assigned advisor going by the alias of Symes, to find evidence on the terrorist (individual or group) who caused a bomb explosion during a presumably peaceful protest in the populated Freedom Plaza in Bonton, the capital city of The Nation, destroying a statue and killing several people. The player soon stumbles upon an activist group called Thought who advocates for freedom of speech with anti-governmental sentiments, yet unaware of Orwell, who is entangled in the bombing incident. From there on, the player uses everything at their disposal to find evidence to expectantly incriminate their first suspect, Cassandra Watergate, an artist who was present at the Plaza shortly before the explosion.

The story occurs across five days (episodes) and what originally seemed like another day at the office, turns into an intricate roller-coaster of a journey full of conspiracy theories, deception and shocking revelations. The narrative in Orwell is exceptionally well-written and what keeps the player on their toes and constantly engaged. Just as things might get slightly monotonous now and again, the story always seems to throw you a new bone through unexpected plot twists and interestingly branched out paths shaped by your various choices and consequences. Even though the story occurs across a country, Orwell actually focuses on a small group of individuals despite the illusion it might give in the beginning, thus I did end up wishing more citizens were actually involved in the end. Whilst this is somewhat disappointing, it makes for a more focused story and does help to get better attached to those said characters, which Orwell succeeds in both aspects. Frankly, the overarching story and its thought-provoking themes, along with the interesting characters you encounter along your journey, albeit a touch stereotypical once in a while, are the selling points of Orwell, and I am delighted to report that it satisfied my itch for a robust adventure mystery game which I have not had for a while recently. Due to the nature of the game, I cannot talk more about the story nor discuss its outcomes at this point, as it is best to unravel and experience it yourself, but there are about four confirmed endings. The game’s length lies somewhere between 4 – 6 hours, which I personally completed in one sitting thanks to its captivating story which made me impatiently want to know what happens next, but I do wish it were longer.

All in all, Orwell's gameplay is akin to a visual novel, so there is not a lot of interactivity involved, but what it does, mechanically speaking, is very solid and straightforward. During investigations, the player has to do various tasks such as (1) browsing and reading through news articles, social media pages and databases, (2) hacking computers or mobile phones to access stored data, and (3) wiretapping conversations over the phone and messaging applications. Each one of these tasks displays various text passages in the form of datachuncks (highlighted by the game for the player’s ease) which could be uploaded on the surveillance system to piece together clues, construct evidence on suspects and, in theory, incriminate them. Each new datachunck uploaded updates a suspect’s profile with more information and occasionally even opens up profiles of new suspects in connection to the respective suspect as the plot thickens. You cannot undo an upload, so think carefully beforehand. Sometimes suspects give contradicting statements over the duration of the story through either dishonesty or unintended misinformation as the result of human nature, which you would then have to use your own judgement and decide which datachunck to upload to support the government’s case, or not. You see, the player can play by the rules to appease the government or ignore vital information to protect the suspects (depending on your moral compass), and either playstyle has several cleverly written consequences. The mechanics do feel too simplistic and repetitive but begin to shine in the second half of the game once there is a lot more information to chew and digest. Moreover, the adviser gives you bite-sized info as to what is happening during almost each one of your moves, so technically you should not feel lost with how the story unfolds. Plus, at the end of each day, a window summary displays all your findings and events that occurred on the day to be up to speed.

One major criticism I do have with its gameplay, however, is that despite the game warning the player that they are not required to upload every datachunk spotted, I always had the compulsion to upload everything I could find regardless since there is no penalty for doing so as far as I recall, aside for a handful of contradictions and, of course, the path of some key plot events. Retrospectively, I feel the game should have better incentivised the player to upload fewer datachuncks or increased contradictions to spice things up. Unfortunately, the game limits your number datachuncks uploads to create a nerve-wracking atmosphere (commendable mechanic) only at the end and I wish that was predominant throughout the entire game instead.

Visually, Orwell is all about the graphical user interface (of a computer monitor) since that is where you will be carrying out all your investigations and decision-making. The art style with its stylized polygonal pictures suits its dystopian themes and the presentation is sufficiently appealing thanks to its good use of appropriate colour pallets and well-designed page layouts. The interface is also intuitive and easy to navigate as a result of its slick design. Whilst the soundtrack is rather short and may seem minimal, it brilliantly captures the eerie atmosphere and even gets momentarily tenser when a plot twist occurs and stakes have risen. Considering there is plenty of reading and no voice acting involved, the tone and vibe of the soundtrack help it to never become distracting.

In conclusion, Orwell: Keeping An Eye On You is a fantastic, but short, mystery game set in a frightfully believable dystopian setting with a strong narrative that challenges your own ethics and presents balanced points of view in the long-lasting battle between the individual’s freedom and privacy versus the government’s security and surveillance. Whilst it is mechanically simplistic and not as diverse, nor challenging, as a game like Papers Please which shares a few familiar social commentaries, it is unique in its own right and worthy of a spiritual successor to 1984. At the end of the day, it is an interactive book more than a conventional adventure game where you might solve puzzles, which feels appropriate considering it is inspired by a novel. Definitely a must-play for George Orwell fans like myself and anyone interested in good mystery/detective games in the format of visual novels.

Stay vigilant.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[b]Believable writing and gameplay mesh to bring the Orwellian nightmare to life.[/b]

[u][i]Summary:[/i][/u]
With [i]Orwell[/i] literally simulating a job, its success or failure as a game almost entirely hinges on the strength of its writing. Fortunately for all of us, it succeeds with flying colors. The characters it depicts are distinct and memorable. The scenarios it presents to you demand your full attention, else you miss something that leads to catastrophe. In the end it will leave you wondering how else things could have played out.

To be clear, [i]Orwell[/i] is an almost entirely text based experience. It mimics a work computer, including internet browser, email, and even a news and weather report. There is no voice acting, though the voice in my head for each of them is so strong that I had to pause and double check myself on that. Props again to the writers for that. The sound in the game sets a good atmosphere but is limited in quantity to the point of being noticeably repetitive.

If you can stomach the reading load, [i]Orwell[/i] is a novel game that is well worth your time and the cost of admission.

[u][i]Additional details:[/i][/u]
The visual style of [i]Orwell[/i] does an excellent job of being familiar enough to reality while also smoothing over reality's rough edges and mismatching designs. Throughout the game you'll uncover multiple pictures of the same character, often showing different sides of the person than you've seen before. For example you may first discover a finely manicured business photo before later discovering a photo of the same person out on the town, presumably a few drinks in and having a good time. Of course these aren't real photos, but artist renditions.

In order to discuss this next topic, I'll give you the most basic, spoiler free description of what you do in the game. You are tasked with investigating specific people and deciding whether what you find does or does not get added to a government database. Essentially you are both the spy and the filter between your target and the government. With that said, there were a few instances related to this that hampered my immersion. Generally it came from being required to enter a piece of information into the Big Brother system that I would have elected to keep private had it not been needed to progress.

I'll close with a few words on replayability. While there are multiple endings and outcomes to each chapter, I personally didn't feel compelled to replay more than a couple specific moments. The decisions that lead to each result are rarely obvious, so it's hard to go back and change things without reexamining things on a larger scale than I was interested in. There are guides out there that could speed up the process if you're so interested. I happily spent 9 hours with [i]Orwell[/i], nearly all of which was a single careful playthrough.

review_text_raw:
This game is very unique and interesting, it is not very long but it is a game that makes you think for a long periods of time.

Pros:
Amazing plot, there are alternative paths
Good choice with factions, there is no 'Good' guys vs 'Bad' guys feeling. Its up to you to create who is 'Good' and who is 'Bad.' This is very good since most recent games are forced to have forced 'Political Correctness.' This game is not bias in politics, and gives choice to player to do what they want and judge how they want. (Think of this game like in Far Cry 4 in terms of factions, you get to judge who is more 'right' or less 'wrong')
Lots of data-based reading (if you are okay with reading lots of things for lore, this is a type of game for you)
Lots of characters to anaylize and discover
Price is very cheap during discount
When you finish the game get ready to have several minutes or hours of heavy philosophical discussion with your mind

Neutral:
They could of added a bit more creative names for the country and political party in the game, all the other nations in game got more creative names while you just live in 'The Nation.' Sadly no Oceania vibes
Pretty good music, I really love intro music but music gets a bit repetitive during the Missions.

Cons:
You have to finish the game to go back to 'Days', if you accidently did something wrong you have to stay all day
I wish more touch was added to characters that got prisoned etc., it just feels awkward not getting a lot of info about them after a certain mission.
Sadly the game is not very long, if you play entire day you can finish the game in one or 2 days (Game is made of 5 Days)

The game is very good, and you should buy it for a nice philosophical experience with your mind.

review_text_raw:
[h1] Final Verdict: Buy [/h1]

Game took me 4 hours to complete 1 playthrough, although you can do multiple playthroughs, depending on what information you find and what connections you make. This game is reading intensive, as you will be sifting through web pages, call logs, chat logs, browser histories, etc. There's also quite a bit of filler information, which is to be expected in this kind of job where you are aggregating huge amounts of data and your job is to sift through that information and find the relevant information.

Not every piece of date is true. There are dead ends and outright lies. Your job will be to try to paint an accurate portrait for your agency to do its job correctly. This game does a great job of putting you in the center of the action as you feel as though you are a real investigator. As the story progresses, you become an even bigger part of the action.

This game isn't for everyone. The gameplay mechanic itself can get tedious at varying times. You really don't stray from what you're doing from the start of Chapter 1 all the way to the conclusion in Chapter 5. So if you don't like parsing information, you will be bored. However, the story keeps it all together and gives purpose to your actions. 

[b]Rate 7/10. Really solid game, interesting story, great ending(s), but the gameplay could have used more variety.[/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Conflict:  Orwell is an excellent game that is well designed and well written. 

Conflict: Orwell is a poorly written game that is horribly designed. 

Choose one. 

Orwell is a game that would demand someone choose one of these options, and the problem is is Orwell is an very good game, that is well written.  It however has some horrible design choices that stop me from calling it excellent or perfect.  In fact these design choices are VERY problematic. 


The entire game of Orwell is viewing webpages/conversations/phone calls and hunting down information and uploading it to a major database.  You're allowed free access to almost anything and you can upload almost anything to the database and play with it.  You'll get chastised for uploading garbage information, but it's also kind of fun.  Then the government who hired you to find the information will eventually operate on what you have found.   The story is told through these uploads and the results of your information gathering will change the story.  That's kind of cool. 

And Orwell tells a compelling (if a little predictable) story.  However it ends abruptly and seems to think it's ending can be a lot more impactful than it ends up being.   And then it falls into an egregious hole of pushing replayability but not allowing players to replay part of the story. 

But the thing is Orwell doesn’t really explain it’s gameplay.  The core of the gameplay is not what you upload, but rather what you choose not to upload, or how you choose to resolve conflicts.   But I really hate how it handles conflicts.  What it should do is allow you to upload conflicting information and have you choose how to resolve it explaining more “what do you think?”  Instead it makes this assumption that A or B is right and whichever you choose, they kind of operate on.  However that’s not how the world works, there’s conflicts in a single paragraph and the question is does the guy feel remorseful or does the guy feel responsible for the past… the answer is probably both, why make me choose. 

Then there’s other conflics that seem to not matter.  But what’s really important is what doesn’t get uploaded, and that’s kind of the problem. 

The first game you’re going to upload everything, because that’s what you think is right, but the game is VERY interesting when you don’t upload everything, you can change the game and the story minorly because of this.  You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. 

Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens.   I just want more interactivity in the story. 

The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent.  This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator.  I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. 

You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same.  In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. 

But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like.  There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story.  Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines.  And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time.  

However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it.  I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay.  I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive.

Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did.  I liked it that much.  10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale.  It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state.  But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. 

I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy.  Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so.

If you enjoyed this review or want to see what other games I enjoyed you can find my curator page at this link. http://store.steampowered.com/curator/31803828-Kinglink-Reviews/ Give me a follow.

You WILL end at the same point, but there is changes that happen. Sadly, the ending is a trinary Mass Effect style choice, that feels a bit eyerolling, even the “this ending is only unlocked if X” doesn’t happen and the end is really two or three screens. I just want more interactivity in the story. The other problem is the final episode is actually excellent. This is the episode where the game shines in a brand new way, it adds a new twist and limits the operator. I almost wish this twist was added in day two or day three because it makes it much more intense to decide what you do, and I’d have liked to see the decisions on day 2 or 3 affect the ending, perhaps locking off the good ending if you fail. You see, the game feels a bit like the Teltale games, low interactivity, always reach the same ending and while that’s true, it’s not the same. In Telltale, the same things happen no matter what, but in this game, there is changes, I just wish there was bigger meaningful changes that persisted, or even changed the ending and I’m hopeful for the future of Orwell because of that. But the story itself is good, if not as interactive as you like. There’s good story twists, there’s good characters, and I actually like everyone involved in the story. Orwell is supposed to be about the surveillance state, and even in that way Orwell shines. And at 5 hours for a full gameplay it might seem expensive, but it can easily be played a second time. However replayability does suck, almost the entire game is the same and you have to play at least 3 or 4 hours to replay it. I wish each episode would be replayable separate so I could go get the three endings of episode 3 and 5 without the full replay. I didn’t mind a second replay but the third is abusive. Overall though I DO like Orwell, the litmus test for this game is “did I put season 2 on my wish list” and I did. I liked it that much. 10 bucks seems high but I think it’s worth the money, and even if not you can get it on sale. It’s a unique experience, and a fun and interesting take on the surveillance state. But even my complaint about the design and the way the game really presents it’s gameplay doesn’t ruin and interesting and engaging story. I’m hopeful, I want to see season 2 have more interactivity, I want to see season 2 involve more limitations on the user, and I want season 2 to be better, but for a first season of a rather novel game type, I’m pretty happy. Orwell delivers what it intends to and I do adore how it does so. As a player you take on the role of a Big Brother investigator in the dystopian world of The Nation, employing Orwell, an information gathering and surveillance software to spy on people. Every datachunk you choose to upload to Orwell has consequences.

The game's minimalist interface, immersive gameplay and intriguing storyline are highly enjoyable, but there are certain areas that could certainly be improved: the tedious and non-skippable dialogues, somewhat abrupt endings and limited control over the game's progression.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell stars you, the player, as an investigator in the Nation's (a stand-in for an unholy almagamation of the United States and the United Kingdom) new, government-ordained spying programme. Your job is to investigate suspected terrorists and cherrypick data you've acquired via researching the Internet and spying directly on their conversations, phones, and computers. You upload these data modules to the Orwell database and help construct a profile of these suspects that your advisor (who can't see your research sources in an effort to maintain some sort of ethical loophole) then uses to report back to the authorities, thus causing your actions to have potentially devastating consequences.

I've seen a few people complain about the gameplay--you are, essentially, dragging these data modules from one part of your screen to another (and, frustratingly, it can take a few clicks to get hold of them), which sounds unexciting on paper. But the story is compelling, and it's through this (slightly repetitive and boring) gameplay that you unlock the story, which can branch depending on which data you upload to Orwell. Some of it you have to, some of it you don't--and some of it you can use to alter the perception of certain suspects by picking which element of contradicting data you want to show to the advisor. 

The game does a very good job of highlighting how people become complacent with this level of privacy invasion--I've seen complaints of the game handholding you throughout, but, in my opinion, this helps you to slip into the mindset of uploading whatever data you come across, mindlessly painting suspects as victims because it's what your advisor wants of you. It wasn't until the end of my first playthrough that I realised how much damage I'd caused by providing evidence to suggest that innocent people were guilty of crimes they hadn't committed, and how many of the characters I'd either had arrested or killed via my actions of "innocuously" collecting their data. Which I guess is what the game wants you to do, particularly on a first playthrough.

That's not to say I don't have complaints. The game wants you to play multiple playthroughs, even if only to collect all of the achievements (most of which can be acquired in two playthroughs; two require a third, or replaying chapters on one of your profiles). Different actions have different outcomes and dialogue, and that produces slightly new scenes to watch (or, really, read). The problem is that the texts and calls you have to monitor can be so tediously long, particularly with little deviation--the last chapter has one that's just about shy of 10 minutes, and you can't do anything but sit and let it play. There's no option to skip the scene. 

I've also seen a few people complain that the game thinks people can never lie or exaggerate, which I assume refers to options where you can report suspects for having outspoken anti-government tendencies... but again, I think this is overlooking what the game wants you to consider. 

I highly recommend Orwell, although I bought it in the Humble Bundle and so bought it for much cheaper than its standard price--and I've already collected all the achievements in just over 6 hours of play, which isn't quite a £1 = 1 hour of playtime at its normal price. It's obviously not a game that's appealing to everyone, but I do think for those that like immersive visual novels with political themes (and that's essentially what it is), you'll enjoy Orwell.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Short, simple and yet so very much worth it.[/h1]

[i]Orwell[/i] places the player in a role of an investigator for a mass surveillance system of the same name. After being assigned a case, the investigator's job is to gather information related to it using means provided by the system - relevant websites, private chats and so on. Information gathered is passed along to an 'adviser' who provides feedback and proceeds with other actions if necessary.

[u]The gameplay itself is rather simplistic.[/u] Shortly put, it consists of a lot of reading and putting highlighted information into the system (with a mere hold'n'drag method), though some of the data may conflict with each other and it will be up to the player to decide which information is correct. I do agree with those who say that [u]the mechanics could be improved[/u], as there is only a small amount of any form of detective work for the player to perform and some may feel like their hand is being held way too often. I should definitely mention though that [u]your choices do matter and influence the story.[/u]

Since I have mentioned it, it would be unforgivable not to say that [u]I found the story incredibly engaging[/u]. The [u]high-level of character development[/u] kept on working me over and over, changing how I feel about specific characters, making me alternate between love and hate for them, leading me on thinking I might have figured out the bad guy only to be presented an even more attractive suspect. 
One bad thing about it? [u]I completed the game in about four hours[/u], which is a liiittle bit short..

[u]The art style itself is very appealing, something which can also be said about the soundtrack[/u] (though do keep in mind it's meant to serve as background music - don't expect high energy or colourfulness!)

I don't think I would be too far off if I called [i]Orwell[/i] a novel which slowly unfolds itself before the player. In my opinion [u]it is a really great experience[/u] and [b]the developers released a demo version[/b] - make sure to play it to see if the game is for you! If you still have your doubts, which are very much understandable due to the simplistic gameplay, consider getting it on sale. It's worth it.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell takes sort of a visual novel framework and bends it until it looks something like a mass surveillance simulator. You're a foreign contractor working within a series of ethical safeguards to perform ethical mass surveillance (if such a thing is possible) for another country's government. And it's an interesting time to be an Orwell contractor, because The Nation is in the grips of a terrorist bombing spree. Your actions and possibly even inaction can bend the arc of the story.

Like most visual novels, your actions don't have major impacts on larger direction of the plot, but they change the details along the way and might make you more sympathetic to ending the game in one way or another. It's neat to go back and see how changes affect things and unlock other achievements, but it does get a little tedious since waiting through real-time chat and phone conversations is a lot less exciting the second time around.

Overall, I had a pretty good time, but most people will probably be one-and-done and put up fewer hours accordingly. Weigh that against how much you're willing to spend.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I mean, we're basically living in a world where we're being tracked and viewed as corporate commodities, so this game isn't much of a stretch. Still, I found myself really enjoying Orwell - so much so that I purchased the next game in the series (Ignorance is Strength) shortly after completing it. The basic premise behind Orwell is that you're an investigator snooping on your fellow citizens in order to connect the dots behind a larger conspiracy. Your choices, of course, will have an impact on the game's ending; they'll also decide the fate of individual characters - whether they escape, get arrested, or even die. The storyline is interesting and presents you with a lot of ethical dilemmas; things are never black and white, although you can certainly make some intriguing choices trying to adhere to such a worldview.

Overall, I don't have many complaints about the game itself. The UI is pretty slick and easy to navigate. Music is nice. However, I wish there was a way to easily skip/speed through phone calls and such. If you want to unlock every achievement, then you'll need to play through the game 3 or 4 times; having the ability to skip or speed through certain dialogues/events would make that feel less cumbersome. I mean, it's worthwhile to replay the game just to see what happens when you make different choices or approach situations from another perspective; it can just feel a bit tedious when you're looking for a specific achievement.

As an added bonus, the second game in the series (Orwell: Ignorance is Strength) takes the events of the first game into consideration. You can even import your investigator's decisions, allowing you to relive the events of the first game while playing through the second. I won't spoil anything, but I like that the developer made that decision; it ties the games together nicely. I'd recommend this game for fans of the cyberpunk/dystopian genres, especially - you'll definitely appreciate the themes and overall feel of the game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]A memorable and engaging experience.[/h1]

Orwell puts you in the shoes of an investigator working for a police state. The goal is to identify and build a case against suspected terrorists using both publicly available and personal/confidential information. Information you upload enables access to further sources. Uploading mention of a notable injury will unlock access to the person's medical records; finding a phone number or email lets you spy in on their correspondence etc. 

But information you upload could be incorrect, or misinterpreted/twisted to suit the government's agenda. How far will you go? Who will you condemn?

[h1]How is it?[/h1]

This core is compelling and unique enough to carry the game through to its conclusion. The comparisons to Papers Please are obvious, but Orwell is far more expansive. Where Papers Please created tension by pitting you against a time limit, Orwell creates a complex, intriguing and politically relevant narrative where you never truly know who is or isn't guilty. It is hard to discuss in detail without spoiling, but the story is full of twists and turns and finds a way to successfully play out dramatic scenes that you experience from behind the safety of your computer screen and the shield of Orwell.

The soundtrack compliments the game nicely, and is used effectively to punctuate important revelations in the story.

It's entirely text-based, and game length depends entirely on your reading speed and habits. Speed-reading and scanning for pertinent information (which the game highlights for you) can shorten the game to 3-4 hours. A more thorough and careful reading, especially if read aloud, can extend your playtime to 8 hours. The game will be a one-time experience for most players, but the game lets you play each episode individually once cleared, and there's enough agency in what optional & conflicting information you upload that replayability is there for those that want it.

[h1]However[/h1]

The game has enough flaws to feel like it wasn't thoroughly tested.

Conflicting information is highlighted in yellow, rather than blue. You can only upload one of these, so the game highlights conflicting information before you've identified what it conflicts with. This is both a minor spoiler and very awkward, and could have easily been handled better.

It's easy to get overwhelmed with information. The game highlights sources with new information for you, but distinguishing between what is optional and mandatory to upload is not obvious. Perhaps this is intentional, but it is too easy to be stuck in a deadlock with 30 possible sources to go through trying to find the one piece of mandatory information you refrained from uploading the first time. An additional icon highlighting old sources with uploadable information would have made this much less tedious.

Spying in on peoples phone conversations happens in real time. This has a wonderful voyeuristic feel to it, but the conversations progress far too fast to read aloud at a comfortable speaking pace. This would be fine if they didn't contain time-sensitive information that needs to be uploaded during the conversation itself. Anyone streaming this or reading aloud to themselves will be caught in the awkward spot of either missing the window to upload information, or have to voice act far too fast for the conversation to sound natural.

Finally, the writing itself is simply poor. I wonder if it was written by a native English speaker or a trained writer. The grammar is awkward, misleading or just incorrect far too often, and this does detract from the otherwise believable world and engaging story the game creates. Simple proof-reading would have solved this.

None of these are game-breaking or significantly ruin the game, but all are so needless, so simply and easily solved that their inclusions are frustrating.

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

If you liked Papers Please, find the theme compelling or want a unique text-based game, you'll enjoy this. It comes with too many niggling issues to recommend at full price, but with a small discount this will be a worthwhile experience that will stay with you for years to come.

review_text_raw:
An interesting, story rich game that strives to challenge your detective skills and question your morales in every decision you make. The choices you make affect the characters and events that happen in the game in a major way and you are always caught questioning if saying one thing about a character will screw over an another one.
The Orwellian vibe is pulled off extremely well with the modern dystopian future, I definitely recommend checking this game out if you are a fan of 1984 as well as casual, story based games. 

The only thing to complain about here is the "call" cutscenes are unskippable, which isn't a problem in itself if you plan on going through the game once, but in order to get all of the achievements in the game, for the endings, you must play through it more than once and without spoiling anything there is a five minute unskippable cutscene involved in every single time you want to get a new ending, by the end of it you can memorise just about every single word said in the conversation and it becomes less fun and more tedious.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is unique and refreshing

Think Emily's Away, except that instead of BEING those angsty young adults who are chatting and calling about their lives, you're intecepting and logging the information that you can gain from those conversations to solve a series of terrorist attacks. 

Think 1984, except that this totalatarian regime was a bit late and only rose after the internet was developed and its only really in one country. 

Think Papers Please, except that instead of working at the border you're working in the equivalent of the Ministry of Truth, and instead of being influnced by the events around you, you're influencing them. 

If you enjoyed any of those titles, I suggest you at least check out the demo. 

The one thing that I have to say about this game is a replay system where you have to go back to the very beginning. Yes, it's authentic, but when you have to go all the way back to the beginning to see what happens when you make a different choice is first of all annoying, and second of all leads to rushing through the previous steps to get to that scenario and that makes it simply tedious.

review_text_raw: I'm torn about whether or not to recommend this game. While the story has an intriguing premise and I enjoyed learning about the different characters, I was a bit disappointed. As others have mentioned, the story is quite linear and there's no point in replaying it. If you do, you can't skip the long conversations, an element that becomes tedious and annoying. This game has great potential, but I wish it offered a greater variety of paths, endings, and choices. Another issue is that there is no way to tell what information you have to process and what information is unnecessary. For this reason, you can find yourself stuck at parts, unsure of what information you're missing to trigger the next scene. At full price, I do not recommend this game. However, if you can grab it at a discounted rate, I'd say go for it. It is an enjoyable little game that is definitely worth one playthrough, but it can be slow paced at times and there's little to no point in replaying it.

Note: One of my friends bought me this since it was on my wishlist, which is why it was marked as free. I was planning on buying it myself though.

I honestly loved this game more than I expected. Though it's not terribly long (I beat it in five hours), it's amazing to go through the game and see all the twists and turns it throws at you. There's so many ways to do everything and your choices on what info to send DO matter. Every little bit of detail can change the end story and it's amazing. I've played various parts multiple times so far after the intial playthrough in order to get the various achievements and I am not disappointed.

The only thing I didn't like about this game is that it isn't as replayable as I'd like. It's not something like "Papers, please", which is what I thought it was. It's a semi-linear story where your choices affect what you can do later on, however there is a story you're forced to travel on. Though I'd like one where you could replay it over and over, I do realize that people like me would be stuck here for a very long time writing down details on anyone and everyone we come across just in case that information somehow becomes relevant at some point.

Overall, I'd give it a 9.5/10 and I've already put the new one on my wishlist, which I plan on buying once it comes out.

Edit: I didn't put this in the inital review,  but after thinking about it I realized that part of the reason I liked this is that it has to deal with things that happen in the world. For example, it has almost an identical copy of what happened to Snowden. The game itself teaches about real life events and politics while making it fun and enjoyable.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I don't review games very often, but I felt that I needed to throw out my two cents on this game. I haven't read any other reviews, so I'm not influenced by what other people think of it.

I went into this game almost entirely blind. I got it a long while ago, and just got around to installing and playing it today. I sat down to give it a quick try, see if I would enjoy it, and ... 3 hours later, I finished the story. It's not a sprawling 100 hour experience, but those 3 hours were intense, and I was locked into the events the entire time.

A brief summary: you play an Investigator using a program called Orwell, which sifts through social media profiles and newspaper articles (and maybe listens in on a few phone calls) to try to track down criminals. Specifically, a bomb has gone off in a public plaza, and you need to find out who did it.

There are some great twists and turns along the way, and I enjoyed myself the entire time. One moment in particular had me literally on the edge of my seat, biting my lip while I listened to a conversation unfold, unable to do anything but wait to see what would happen. This was a conversation that only occurred because of choices that I had made, and in the end, I had to live with the consequences of those choices. It was rough, and it was emotional, but it was amazing.

Anyway, I love this game. I give it a 4/5 on my "arbitrary 5 point rating scale". The writing felt a little clunky at times, which is really the only complaint that I have, and it's not bad enough to really detract from the experience. Please give this game a try!

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
There are many identities that you can choose at the start of the game.
I chose to become a grandma.
On the internet, no one knows you're a grandma.

Jokes aside, Orwell captures what I love most about indie games: a simple idea that invokes thoughts and feelings.

Orwell provides a nice overview of the current state of our privacy: constantly surveillanced, seldom noticed.
I backed two other similar games on Kickstarter (Top Secret and Need To Know) wishing for the same thing I can feel playing this game: the responsibility (or the lack thereof) of spying on other's privacy, and deciding how they should be looked at or dealt with: a small oversight on a character's relationship status could make me think about it till the end of the game. Even though such details may not be important to the story, it still bothered me: because it is the identity that I altered, and there was no turning back. It fits well with doublethink, and made me Winston: I might be the only one who knows the truth that he is divorced, but to everyone else, he is still married (this circumstance did not sound familiar until I wrote that line down, makes me curious if the given decision is put in delibrately). And this thought is freightening; because "he might be alone in holding that belief, and if alone, then a lunatic... the horror was that he might also be wrong." This thought of people not caring about this as it serves no function, and the possibility that I might be actually wrong and it really does not matter, troubles me greatly.

The mechanics are similar to what workers do at Recdep, but of course not entirely, as the purpose of Recdep does not fit the current state of politics nor the theme of this game. Instead of altering history, we are 'phrasing' history, finding quotes which can be used for our advantage and possibly against our target, the quotes may not need to be said seriously or truthfully, nor are they meant to be always perceived literally, but we use them all the same: perhap an alternate form of "the indifference of reality". Although not altering history in any way, you are still creating history, and that is very doublethink.

Choices. Whether this is not Ingsoc is debatable, as there are preferable choices and crimethink for Ingsoc. However, choices in Orwell definitely allow the player to be as Orwellian as they wish to be, in terms of accusations. You can charge a person with crime from a single sentence and thought, some may not even be said seriously. Of course, Orwell needs to allow you the freedom of choice, because our current state of freedom allows it, or as we think. Nevertheless, the ultimate choice is still yours. In my first playthrough I decided to unbellyfeel my superior. Perhaps I will do something else next time.

Overall, this game at least is able to capture the Orwellian idea of possible surveillance and control, while attempts to inform the players that we may still have the ultimate power of choice. Whether of not this game will still ring true 4 years later is uncertain for me at the moment, but as a person who loves Nineteen Eighty-Four, I am happy to see that people can make an effort to prove that oldthinkers unbellyfeel Ingsoc.

(4 years later: fortunately not)

review_text_raw:
So I just finished my second playthrough and I'm highly inclined to replay it again in order to get another ending. I find Orwell to be a fantasticly entertaining game that tested my attention and combination skills. I really liked the case and the parts of the story that turned out slightly different whenever I did or didn't upload certain data chunks. The endings were frustratingly unsatisfying but because of that all the more realistic and refreshing - so far there was no possible way to have an entirely 'good' ending because no matter what there was always something not sitting well with my conscience. I applaud the developers for daring to leave some kind of open ending to the game.

The only thing I found annoying was that whenever I didn't pay enough attention to what data I was uploading and uploaded information that was false or misleading, I couldn't revert the change and I had to replay the entire chapter to get to the same point again. Which sometimes led to me making the same mistake AGAIN because I clicked through all of it too fast without paying attention, so I had to repeat the same thing again. I know the game tells you to stay on your guard in order to avoid uploading bullshit data, but a simple 'delete data' or 'change data' button would have made this a lot easier.

Oh yeah, the topic of government surveillance as portrayed throughout the game was both intriguing and scaring. It makes you wonder how far governments in real life intend to go in order to guarantee for their respective nations' security. No matter what your opinion on this matter is, there's no saying in what the 'correct' procedure is - spying on every citizen and evaluating on that base is no solution, but neither is leaving people to their own devices and letting potential threats go unchecked.

To everyone interested in this topic, I would highly recommend this fantastic game.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game really does sell the vibe that you're an analyst working inside of Orwell's system, while never feeling tedious or contrived, a big achievement in my book. But of course, the real pull of a game like this is its ability to explore difficult themes about freedom of expression, security, surveillance, checks and balances, etc...

I found the narrative compelling and nuanced. The gameplay effectively branches narratives based on the prejudices of the player and it was interesting to see how an individual with different philosophies might simply follow a different rabbit hole, never stumbling upon the same "truths" that I had. In presenting the narrative this way, the creators wrote a fair bit of nuance into the story: little arcs that can be easily missed if someone's inclined one way or another on a controversial subject. The tension between the themes is reasonably well managed and the endings express different morals; I find the decision to not conclusively state a moral position to be quite brave from the creators' parts and such a decision serves the broader concept of the game very well. 

In considering games as art, I think Orwell provides an excellent example of an expression that is best explored through the medium of video games. Orwell feels like a fledgling OS, simple, sleek, intuitive as an Apple product, creepy and intrusive as a Google one. As a user, you are complicit in the structures of surveillance and, while you have some authority on how to navigate the complex moral questions in front of you (and in doing so, revealing your own biases), there is a palpable sense that this apparatus is large, amorphous, and exuding a sense of clinical evil that only exists with oppressive regimes or corporations. In other words, this game conveys appropriately both the individual and systemic realities of mass surveillance. Now onto my main gripe.

The characters are all viciously annoying human beings. While I certainly understand that in order to create a game with significant nuance in the face of large, controversial themes, individual characters almost necessarily have to retain both positive and negative qualities (a very human characterization), I nevertheless ended up finding the characters insufferable. If my ID had its way, these asshats would all be jailed simply for being pompous, room-temperature IQ, morons with the total and absolute inability to make a single correct decision in their lives. Even characters I initially found likeable or at least, found myself agreeing with, ended up talking their way into these childish and absurd holes and given that the characters are crucial to the gameplay and their interactions are the basis for plot advancement, I often found reading their texts quite a drag. 

Overall, a solid exploration of difficult themes through a very effective medium. Props to the creators for their creativity, narrative complexity, and willingness to engage with controversial subjects without tribalism or devolving into virtue-signaling. I especially like how the game exposes your own biases (though never in an explicit manner). May Hancock slowly rot into agonizing, ego-shattering insanity as he's thrown into the darkest dungeon.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Simply one of the best games I've played all year. As an IT security professional I always find portrayals of concepts like "internet" and "hacking" as pretty hard to swallow in both games and movies, but this games nails surprisingly well both the technical possibilities and the intricate moral dilemmas that arise with them. I've also been surprised by the quality of the script: even though it has some specific set of conclusions in mind, it's open ended enough to accomodate different nuances in the approach to the ethics of "privacy vs security in the age of surveillance".

The musical score deserve a special mention: it keeps you to the edge of the seat and enhances very well whenever you reveal certain pieces of critical information.

It's also worth a couple of replays to see how your actions can have different impacts, but be warned that it gets a bit tedious due to the fact that everything happens in real time and there's no way to speed up some parts (or at least, not obvious). I find the lack of checkpoints somewhat of a feature, since it gives weight to the consequences.

Again, kudos to the writing team for surprising some chilling aspects of the choices faced by all parties involved (and I want to keep this spoiler free, so I'll stop here).

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain
